Add GST vs Remove GST — which mode to use

Add GST (Exclusive) means your starting amount is the pre-tax base price. Use this when you know what something costs before tax and want to find the final price a customer pays. Example: you're a freelancer quoting ₹50,000 for a project and need to add 18% GST to raise an invoice — enter ₹50,000 in Add GST mode and you get ₹59,000 as the total to charge the client.

Remove GST (Inclusive) means your starting amount already includes GST, and you want to find the base price. Use this when you've paid a GST-inclusive price and need to know how much of it was tax, either to claim input tax credit or to record the base amount in accounts. Example: you paid ₹11,800 for a purchase and need to extract the base amount — enter ₹11,800 in Remove GST mode at 18% and you get ₹10,000 as the base, ₹1,800 as the GST paid.

CGST, SGST, and IGST — what goes where

GST revenue is split between the central and state governments, and the split depends on whether the transaction is within one state or crosses state lines.

Intra-state transaction (buyer and seller in the same state): GST is split equally between CGST and SGST. On an 18% transaction, 9% goes to the Centre as CGST and 9% goes to the state government as SGST. Both appear as separate line items on the invoice. The buyer sees two tax lines but pays one combined amount.

Inter-state transaction (buyer and seller in different states, or imports): IGST applies at the full rate — 18% goes entirely to the Centre as IGST, which then distributes the state's share to the destination state. Only one tax line appears on the invoice. All e-commerce sales and most B2B cross-state sales use IGST.

The practical importance: if you're registered for GST, the CGST/SGST/IGST split determines which column you fill in on your GSTR returns. Getting this wrong leads to mismatches during GST filing even if the total tax amount is correct.

GST rate slabs and common goods/services

0% — Fresh produce (vegetables, fruits, milk, eggs), unprocessed grains, healthcare services, education services, public transport. These are GST-exempt, meaning no GST applies and input tax credit cannot be claimed on related inputs.

5% — Packaged branded food items, economy hotel stays (under ₹7,500/night), passenger rail and air economy transport, household goods like sugar and edible oil. Restaurants without AC charge 5% GST (without input tax credit).

12% — Processed foods, computers and accessories, mobile phones, most medicines and pharma products, construction for affordable housing. Business class air travel is also 12%.

18% — The most common rate. Covers most services: IT services, professional services, consultancy, telecom, restaurants with AC, hotel stays above ₹7,500/night, electronic goods, industrial machinery. If you're unsure of a rate, 18% is the most likely answer for services.

28% — Luxury goods, automobiles (cars, motorcycles), cement, tobacco and tobacco products, aerated beverages, casinos and online gaming. Many items in this slab also attract an additional GST Compensation Cess on top of the 28%.

Input Tax Credit (ITC) — what it means for businesses

If you're a GST-registered business, you can offset the GST you paid on purchases (input tax) against the GST you collected from customers (output tax). Only the net amount needs to be deposited with the government. This is what makes GST a "value-added" tax — each link in the supply chain only pays tax on the value it adds, not on the full price.

ITC cannot be claimed on: personal-use expenses, food and beverages (unless you're in the food business), insurance for personal vehicles, construction for own use, and a few other blocked categories under Section 17(5) of the CGST Act. Getting ITC wrong is one of the most common reasons businesses face GST notices.

Frequently asked questions

My invoice shows 9% CGST + 9% SGST. Is the total GST 18% or 9%?

18%. CGST and SGST each show half the applicable rate, but together they equal the full GST rate. A transaction at 18% GST always shows as 9% CGST + 9% SGST for intra-state transactions. The total tax amount is 18% of the base. Some people mistakenly think they're being taxed twice — they're not. It's one 18% tax split between two governments.

When does GST registration become mandatory?

Businesses with annual turnover above ₹40 lakh (goods) or ₹20 lakh (services) must register for GST. In special category states (North-East, Himachal, Uttarakhand, etc.), the threshold is ₹20 lakh for goods and ₹10 lakh for services. E-commerce sellers must register regardless of turnover. If you're doing inter-state supply of goods, registration is mandatory from the first rupee of turnover.

Is GST calculated on the discounted price or original price?

GST is calculated on the transaction value — the actual price charged after any trade discounts that are known at the time of supply and are clearly stated on the invoice. Post-supply discounts (cashbacks, loyalty points) have different treatment. If you sell a product at ₹1,000 with a 10% trade discount shown on the invoice (net ₹900), GST applies on ₹900. If the ₹100 discount is given later as credit, the original ₹1,000 was the transaction value and GST applied on that.

What is the reverse charge mechanism (RCM)?

Normally, the supplier collects and deposits GST. Under the Reverse Charge Mechanism, the recipient (buyer) is liable to pay GST directly to the government instead. RCM applies in specific cases: services from unregistered suppliers to registered businesses above certain thresholds, import of services, GTA (goods transport) services, advocate services, and a few others specified by the government. If RCM applies, the supplier doesn't charge GST on the invoice — the buyer self-assesses and deposits it.
